transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Losing that gallery income has thrown me off so much that I feel like I’m not handling the money stress in a normal way anymore. A close friend actually encouraged me to come in because it's started to feel like too much to handle on my own.

Did these feelings start soon after losing your gallery income, and are they mostly tied to that specific stressor, or do you find yourself worrying or feeling down about many things even apart from it?

Yes, they started almost immediately, within a week or two of finding out the gallery was closing about a month ago. It is completely tied to this financial mess, and I really feel like once I can secure a steady part-time job or a new source of income, this stress will finally ease up.

How has this stress been affecting your day-to-day functioning—for example, your sleep, appetite, ability to work, or relationships? Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn’t worth living?

The stress has made me snap at my partner over tiny things, and I've been avoiding my bills so much that I almost got evicted and even stopped going to my sketching group out of embarrassment. Fortunately, my sleep and appetite are mostly fine, and I absolutely do not have any thoughts of harming myself or feeling like life isn't worth living.

Compared with what most people would be expected to feel after losing a job or income, does your reaction feel clearly stronger or harder to control than you think it should be? Has it caused major problems in work, finances, or relationships beyond the stressor itself?

Yes, it definitely feels much stronger and harder to control than normal; the stress is completely taking over my brain, causing me to panic, snap at my partner, and then just zone out. It has caused major problems, like missing payment deadlines, almost getting a formal eviction warning, and avoiding my usual sketching group because I feel too embarrassed to show up.

final_diagnosis.reason: Symptoms began within 1–2 weeks of an identifiable psychosocial stressor (loss of gallery income/financial crisis), are clearly tied to that stressor, are experienced as disproportionate and hard to control, and have caused significant impairment in finances, relationships, and social functioning. No evidence was provided for suicidality, pervasive symptoms independent of the stressor, or another primary disorder in the interview.
